1.note: Here, the word **saying** introduces a direct quotation. See how you translated **saying** in [1:1](ta:01).

2.note: Here, **the sons of Israel** represents the people or descendants of Israel. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [the people of Israel]

2.q: מַטֶּ֣ה מַטֶּה֩ לְ⁠בֵ֨ית אָ֜ב מֵ⁠אֵ֤ת כָּל־נְשִֽׂיאֵ⁠הֶם֙ לְ⁠בֵ֣ית אֲבֹתָ֔⁠ם שְׁנֵ֥ים עָשָׂ֖ר מַטּ֑וֹת
2.note: If it would be more natural in your language, you may want to put the information about how many staffs there were before the information about whom the staffs represented. You may also be able to combine or shorten some of the phrases. Alternate translation: [12 staffs, one for each of the leaders for the house of each of their fathers]

Here and throughout this chapter, the phrases **house of a father** and **house of their fathers** refer to whole tribes. This is unlike Numbers 3-4, where the phrases refer to the largest divisions within each tribe. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could make that idea more explicit. Alternate translation: [for an ancestral tribe … for each of their ancestral tribes]

If it would be more natural in your language, you may want to put the information about writing before the information about each man’s name. Alternate translation: [You shall write each man’s name on his staff]

3.q: וְ⁠אֵת֙ שֵׁ֣ם אַהֲרֹ֔ן תִּכְתֹּ֖ב עַל־מַטֵּ֣ה לֵוִ֑י כִּ֚י מַטֶּ֣ה אֶחָ֔ד לְ⁠רֹ֖אשׁ בֵּ֥ית אֲבוֹתָֽ⁠ם
3.note: If it would be more natural in your language, you could reverse the order of these phrases, since the second phrase gives the reason for the result that the first phrase describes. Alternate translation: [And because one staff is for the head of the house of their fathers, the name of Aaron you shall write on the staff of Levi]

If it would be more natural in your language, you may want to put the information about writing before the information about the name of Aaron. Alternate translation: [And you shall write the name of Aaron]

By **the staff of Levi**, Yahweh means another staff in addition to the twelve from the previous verse. See the chapter introduction for more information. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [on another staff, the staff of Levi]

Yahweh is using the possessive form to describe a **staff** that is characterized by representing the tribe of **Levi**. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the staff that represents Levi]

Here Yahweh is speaking as if the leader of a tribe were the **head** of a body. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [is for the leader of]
See how you translated this phrase in verse 2. Alternate translation: [each ancestral tribe]

4.note: Here, **face** represents the area in front of the **Testimony**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [before the Testimony]

Here, **the Testimony** means the Ten Commandments, and here it refers to the box or chest that contained the Ten Commandments. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [the box that contained the Testimony] or [the box with the Ten Commandments in it]

Here, the pronoun **you** is plural and refers to Moses and the representatives of Israel. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [where I meet with all of you there]

5.note: Here Yahweh is speaking as if the **murmurings** of the Israelites were a physical burden resting **upon** him. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And I will end the murmurings of the sons of Israel that trouble me]

The word translated as **And** indicates that what follows is a result of what came before. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that what follows is a result of what came before. Alternate translation: [As a result, I will cause to subside]

5.q: תְּלֻנּוֹת֙ בְּנֵ֣י יִשְׂרָאֵ֔ל אֲשֶׁ֛ר הֵ֥ם מַלִּינִ֖ם עֲלֵי⁠כֶֽם
5.note: Yahweh is using a construction in which a verb and its object come from the same root. You may be able to use the same construction in your language to express the meaning here. Alternatively, your language may have another way of saying this. Alternate translation: [the murmurings of the sons of Israel against you] or [how the sons of Israel murmur against you]
Here, the pronoun **you** is plural and refers to Moses and Aaron. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [against the two of you]

6.q: מַטֶּה֩ לְ⁠נָשִׂ֨יא אֶחָ֜ד מַטֶּ֨ה לְ⁠נָשִׂ֤יא אֶחָד֙
6.note: Here, the author repeats the phrase **a staff for one leader** to indicate that each leader gave one staff. If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [one staff from each of them]
See how you translated the similar expression in 17:2.

Here the author implies that **the staff of Aaron** was an additional staff added to the 12 staffs from the other leaders. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [And the staff of Aaron was placed among the other 12 staffs]

7.note: Here, **face** represents the presence of Yahweh. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [before Yahweh]

The author is using the possessive form to describe **the tent** that contained the **Testimony**, which is the Ten Commandments. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [in the tent that contained the Testimony] or [in the tent in which were the Ten Commandments]

8.note: The author is using the word translated as **it happened** to introduce a new event in the story. Use a word, phrase, or other method in your language that is natural for introducing a new event.

The author is using **from the next day** as a common expression of the culture to mean “on the day after.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [on the day after]
See how you translated this phrase in verse 7.

The author is using **behold** as a common expression of the culture to mean “pay attention to what follows.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and he saw that the staff of Aaron]

The author is not distinguishing this **staff of Aaron** from another staff of Aaron that is not **for the house of Levi**. The author is reminding readers which tribal staff was Aaron’s. Be sure that this is clear in your translation. Alternate translation: [the staff that represented the house of Levi, which was Aaron’s staff,]

8.q: פָּרַ֥ח & וַ⁠יֹּ֤צֵֽא פֶ֨רַח֙ וַ⁠יָּ֣צֵֽץ צִ֔יץ וַ⁠יִּגְמֹ֖ל שְׁקֵדִֽים
8.note: Here, the author could be indicating that all these stages of growth: (1) had happened during the night, and Moses saw the final result: the **almonds**. Alternate translation: [had sprouted, brought out a blossom, blossomed a flower, and finally ripened almonds] (2) were present at one time when Moses saw it. Alternate translation: [was sprouting, bringing out a blossom, blossoming a flower, and ripening almonds almost all at once]

In this verse, the words **blossom** and **flower** are singular in form, but they refer to several blossoms and flowers as a group. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use the plural forms of these words. Alternate translation: [blossoms … flowers]

The author implies that these **almonds**, a kind of nut, were fully ripe. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [almonds to full ripeness]

9.note: Here, **face** represents the presence of Yahweh. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [from before Yahweh]

The author is using **a man his staff** as a common expression of the culture to mean that each man **saw** and **took** his own staff. If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And each one saw and then took his own staff]

10.note: See how you translated the similar expression in 17:4.
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **keeping**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [to be kept]

Yahweh is using **the sons of rebellion** as a common expression of the culture to mean “the people who rebel.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [for the people who rebel]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **rebellion**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [for the rebellious sons]

Here Yahweh is speaking as if the **murmurings** of the Israelites were a physical burden resting **upon** him. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. See how you translated the similar phrase in verse 5. Alternate translation: [And you shall end their murmuring against me]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **murmurings**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the words they murmur]

Here, **and** marks **they shall not die** as the goal or purpose of **you shall finish their murmurings from upon me**. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that this is the purpose. Alternate translation: [and that way, they shall not die]

11.q: וַ⁠יַּ֖עַשׂ מֹשֶׁ֑ה כַּ⁠אֲשֶׁ֨ר צִוָּ֧ה יְהוָ֛ה אֹת֖⁠וֹ כֵּ֥ן עָשָֽׂה
11.note: It might seem that the expression **thus he did** contains extra information that would not be natural to express in your language. If so, you could shorten it. Alternate translation: [And Moses did just as Yahweh had commanded him]

12.note: The Israelites are using the word **Behold** to express a strong feeling of alarm and despair. There may be an equivalent word or phrase in your language that you can use in your translation to convey this feeling. If not, you could say what the Israelites were feeling, or you could say what made them afraid. Alternate translation: [Alas]

The Israelites say **we expire! We perish; all of us perish** as an extreme statement for emphasis. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a different way to express the emphasis. Alternate translation: [we are like those who expire! It is as if we perish, as if all of us perish]

These three phrases **we expire**, **We perish**, and **all of us perish** mean basically the same thing. The repetition emphasizes the meaning by repeating the same idea with different words. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could combine them and express the emphasis in another way. Alternate translation: [We are all going to die!]

13.q: כֹּ֣ל הַ⁠קָּרֵ֧ב הַ⁠קָּרֵ֛ב אֶל־מִשְׁכַּ֥ן יְהוָ֖ה יָמ֑וּת
13.note: The terms **coming near** and **the one coming near** mean similar things. The Israelites are using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [Every single one coming near to the Dwelling of Yahweh will die]

The Israelites are using the question form to express despair. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [We will all finish to expire!]

The Israelities are using **finish to expire** as a common expression of the culture to mean “die.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Shall we end our lives in death] or [Shall we experience death]
